hook.text: Tesla owners woke up one morning to find their cars had gained 50 miles of range overnight—via a software update.

buildup.text: Over-the-air updates let manufacturers change how a car drives, steers, and brakes without visiting a dealer.

discovery.text: This means your car can genuinely improve after you buy it, gaining new features months or years later.

twist.text: But it also means a bad update could disable safety systems for millions of cars simultaneously.

climax.text: Regulators are scrambling to create rules for software updates that can change a car's physical behavior remotely.

punchline.text: Your car updates itself like a phone—with far higher stakes.

quiz.question: What risk do over-the-air car updates introduce?
options: A bad update could affect safety across millions of cars

details.summary: Over-the-air updates let automakers push new software to vehicles remotely, fixing bugs, improving performance, and adding features without requiring a dealership visit.
details.whyItMatters: OTA updates transform cars into upgradable platforms. Tesla famously improved braking distances and added Autopilot features through wireless updates alone.
takeaways: Software patches are downloaded via cellular or Wi-Fi
Updates can improve range, safety, and infotainment
They reduce costly recalls by fixing issues remotely

faq.question: Can an OTA update brick your car?
faq.answer: Automakers use fail-safe mechanisms like dual software partitions so the car can roll back to the previous version if an update fails. Bricking is extremely rare but not impossible.

faq.question: Do all modern cars support OTA updates?
faq.answer: Most new EVs and many premium ICE vehicles now support OTA for infotainment and some vehicle systems. Full powertrain OTA capability varies significantly by manufacturer.
